records.title: Dataset Pruning: Reducing Training Data by Examining Generalization Influence

problem.text: How to construct a smallest subset from the entire training data as a proxy training set without significantly sacrificing the model's performance?

evidence.quote: How much does each individual training sample or a sub-training-set affect the model's generalization, and how to construct a smallest subset from the entire training data as a proxy training set without significantly sacrificing the model's performance?

method.text: An optimization-based dataset pruning method that examines the influence of removing training samples on generalization and constructs a smallest subset with a constrained generalization gap.

evidence.quote: To answer these, we propose dataset pruning, an optimization-based sample selection method that can (1) examine the influence of removing a particular set of training samples on model's generalization ability with theoretical guarantee, and (2) construct a smallest subset of training data that yields strictly constrained generalization gap.

In this work, we present an optimization-based dataset pruning method that can prune a largest subset from the entire training dataset with (a) theoretically guaranteed generalization gap and (b) consideration of the joint influence of all collected data.

results.text: The method prunes 40% of training examples on CIFAR-10, halves convergence time with only 1.3% test accuracy decrease, and is competitive with other baseline methods.

evidence.quote: Furthermore, the proposed method prunes 40% training examples on the CIFAR-10 dataset, halves the convergence time with only 1.3% test accuracy decrease, which is superior to previous score-based sample selection methods.
Superior to previous score-based sample selection methods, our proposed method prunes 40% training examples in CIFAR-10 <cit.>, halves the convergence time, and achieves only 1.3% test accuracy drop.

We show that the test accuracy of a network trained on the pruned dataset is comparable to the test accuracy of the network trained on the whole dataset, and is competitive with other baseline methods.

contributions.text: Proposes a dataset pruning method that extends the sample selection problem from cardinality constraint to generalization constraint.

evidence.quote: Before delving into details, we summarize our contributions as below: * This paper proposes a dataset pruning method, which extends the sample selection problem from cardinality constraint to generalization constraint.

records.title: Deep Learning on a Data Diet: Finding Important Examples Early in Training

problem.text: How much of the data is superfluous, which examples are important for generalization, and how do we find them?

evidence.quote: It is therefore natural to ask: how much of the data is superfluous, which examples are important for generalization, and how do we find them?

method.text: A scoring method based on the initial loss gradient norm of individual training examples to identify important and difficult examples early in training for pruning.

evidence.quote: To address these challenges, we propose a scoring method that can be used to identify important and difficult examples early in training, and prune the training dataset without large sacrifices in test accuracy.

* We propose to score the importance of each training (x_i,y_i) by its expected loss gradient norm (score), which, up to a constant, bounds the expected change in loss for an arbitrary (x,y) caused by removing (x_i,y_i). * We show that pruning training samples with small scores at initialization allows one to train on as little as 50% of the training data without any loss in accuracy (CIFAR-10).

results.text: Pruning training samples with small scores at initialization allows training on as little as 50% of the data without loss in accuracy on CIFAR-10.

evidence.quote: In all experiments accuracies achieved by training on the full dataset and on a random subset of the corresponding size are used as baselines.

problem.text: State-of-the-art coreset selection methods perform well at low pruning rates but struggle at high pruning rates due to poor data coverage.

evidence.quote: State-of-the-art coreset selection methods typically assign an importance score to each example and select the most important examples to form a coreset.

We then propose a new coreset selection method, Coverage-centric Coreset Selection (CCS), where we jointly consider overall data coverage based on the proposed metric as well as importance of each example.

method.text: Coverage-centric Coreset Selection (CCS), which combines data coverage with importance-based sampling using stratified sampling.

evidence.quote: We propose a novel coreset selection method, called Coverage-centric Coreset Selection (CCS), that combines data coverage with importance-based sampling.
We propose the CCS method that adopts a classical idea from statistics: stratified sampling.

results.text: CCS outperforms other baseline methods under high pruning rates and achieves comparable performance for low pruning rates.

evidence.quote: The evaluation results show that CCS outperforms other baseline methods with high pruning rates and achieves comparable accuracy with low pruning rates.

records.title: Data pruning and neural scaling laws: fundamental limitations of score-based algorithms

problem.text: Data pruning algorithms aim to reduce computational costs, but they often fail to outperform random pruning in high compression regimes (30% or less of data kept).

evidence.quote: Data pruning algorithms are commonly used to reduce the memory and computational cost of the optimization process.
The goal of data pruning is to identify a small, yet representative sample of the data that accurately reflects the characteristics and patterns of the entire dataset.

Recent empirical results (<cit.>) reveal that random data pruning remains a strong baseline and outperforms most existing data pruning methods in the high compression regime, i.e. where a fraction of 30% or less of the data is kept.

method.text: The authors introduce a framework for score-based pruning algorithms (geometry-based, uncertainty-based, and error-based) and analyze their asymptotic behavior and distribution shift.

evidence.quote: Our contributions are as follows: * We introduce a new framework for data pruning that encompasses a wide range of popular algorithms (score-based pruning algorithms). * We analyze the asymptotic behavior of algorithms and identify a phenomenon of distribution shift that provably impacts the generalization error. * We demonstrate No-Free-Lunch results that characterize when and why score-based pruning algorithms perform worse than random pruning. * We show that cannot be used in the high compression regime without a significant drop in performance.
These can generally be categorized into four groups: * Geometry based methods: these methods are based on some geometric measure in the feature space.

A similar idea based on the K-centroids of the input data was used in <cit.>. * Uncertainty based methods: the aim of such methods is to find the most “difficult" examples, defined as the ones for which the model is the least confident.

Different uncertainty measures can be used for this purpose, see <cit.> for more details. * Error based methods: the goal is to find the most significant examples defined as the ones that contribute the most to the loss.

records.title: Repeated Random Sampling for Minimizing the Time-to-Accuracy of Learning

problem.text: Existing data pruning and distillation strategies come with high computational costs and often under-perform random sampling in high data compression regimes.

evidence.quote: Methods for carefully selecting or generating a small set of training data to learn from, i.e., data pruning, coreset selection, and data distillation, have been shown to be effective in reducing the ever-increasing cost of training neural networks.

However, these strategies come with additional computational costs associated with subset selection or data distillation before training begins, and furthermore, many are shown to even under-perform random sampling in high data compression regimes.

method.text: The authors introduce Repeated Sampling of Random Subsets (RS2), which samples a subset uniformly at random for each training epoch.

evidence.quote: In this work, we revisit a powerful yet overlooked random sampling strategy to address these challenges and introduce an approach called Repeated Sampling of Random Subsets (RSRS or RS2), where we randomly sample the subset of training data for each epoch of model training.
Motivated by this gap, we introduce Repeated Sampling of Random Subsets (RSRS = RS2), where we sample a subset uniformly at random for each training epoch.

results.text: RS2 reaches higher accuracy than existing methods across a wide range of pruning ratios, trains the fastest, and is robust to noisy labels.

evidence.quote: We show that: * Across a wide range of pruning ratios, RS2 reaches higher accuracy than all existing methods. * For a given pruning ratio, RS2 also trains the fastest, and thus has the fastest time-to-accuracy. * In the presence of noisy labels, RS2 is the most robust data pruning method; It achieves the highest end-model accuracy and lowest relative drop in performance vs. training on the clean dataset.

limitations.text: The authors identify a gap between RS2 and training on the full dataset and seek to overcome limitations of data pruning when training with SGD.

evidence.quote: Specifically, we are excited for future work focused on the following question: How can we further close the gap between RS2 and training on the full dataset?
Can we overcome this limitation of data pruning when training with SGD without eliminating the runtime benefits?

contributions.text: The authors introduce RS2, test it against state-of-the-art methods, and provide a convergence analysis.

records.title: Coverage-centric Coreset Selection for High Pruning Rates

problem.text: State-of-the-art coreset selection methods perform well at low pruning rates but struggle at high pruning rates due to poor data coverage.

evidence.quote: State-of-the-art coreset selection methods typically assign an importance score to each example and select the most important examples to form a coreset.

Inspired by theoretical results, we propose a novel coverage-based metric and, based on the metric, find that coresets selected by importance-based coreset methods at high pruning rates can be expected to perform poorly compared to random coresets because of worse data coverage.

method.text: Coverage-centric Coreset Selection (CCS), which combines data coverage with importance-based sampling using a density-based partial cover metric.

evidence.quote: We propose a novel coreset selection method, called Coverage-centric Coreset Selection (CCS), that combines data coverage with importance-based sampling.

By extending classical geometric set cover to density-based partial cover, we propose a novel data coverage metric and show that existing importance-based coreset selections lead to poor data coverage, which in turn degrades model performance.

results.text: CCS outperforms other baseline methods under high pruning rates and achieves comparable performance for low pruning rates.

evidence.quote: The evaluation results show that CCS outperforms other baseline methods with high pruning rates and achieves comparable accuracy with low pruning rates.

limitations.text: The accuracy drop at high pruning rates is a significant limitation, and finding the optimal hyperparameter beta is left for future work.

evidence.quote: This accuracy drop is a significant limitation as it limits the extent to which coresets can be reduced in size with these selection methods.
We leave how to more efficiently find the optimal β for future work.

contributions.text: Generalizes theoretical bounds for coreset loss to a density-based characterization and proposes the CCS method.

evidence.quote: More specifically, we make the following contributions: * We start by generalizing the result in <cit.>, which provided a probabilistic bound on model loss for a r-cover coreset, where r is the smallest radius around the coreset points that covers 100% of the training set, to a density-based characterization of the coreset in which the radius r is allowed to cover a percentage p of a density space.

We then propose a new coreset selection method, Coverage-centric Coreset Selection (CCS), where we jointly consider overall data coverage based on the proposed metric as well as importance of each example.

problem.text: Data pruning often leads to gradient expectation bias between pruned and original data, preventing lossless performance.

evidence.quote: A common approach is to simply filter out samples that make less contribution to the training.

method.text: InfoBatch, an unbiased dynamic data pruning framework that prunes samples based on loss distribution and rescales gradients of remaining samples.

evidence.quote: To solve this problem, we propose InfoBatch, a novel framework aiming to achieve lossless training acceleration by unbiased dynamic data pruning.

records.title: Data pruning and neural scaling laws: fundamental limitations of score-based algorithms

problem.text: Data pruning algorithms aim to reduce computational costs, but they often fail to outperform random pruning in high compression regimes (30% or less of data kept).

evidence.quote: Data pruning algorithms are commonly used to reduce the memory and computational cost of the optimization process.
The goal of data pruning is to identify a small, yet representative sample of the data that accurately reflects the characteristics and patterns of the entire dataset.

Recent empirical results (<cit.>) reveal that random data pruning remains a strong baseline and outperforms most existing data pruning methods in the high compression regime, i.e. where a fraction of 30% or less of the data is kept.

method.text: The authors introduce a framework for score-based pruning algorithms (geometry-based, uncertainty-based, and error-based) and analyze their asymptotic behavior and distribution shift.

evidence.quote: Our contributions are as follows: * We introduce a new framework for data pruning that encompasses a wide range of popular algorithms (score-based pruning algorithms). * We analyze the asymptotic behavior of algorithms and identify a phenomenon of distribution shift that provably impacts the generalization error. * We demonstrate No-Free-Lunch results that characterize when and why score-based pruning algorithms perform worse than random pruning. * We show that cannot be used in the high compression regime without a significant drop in performance.
These can generally be categorized into four groups: * Geometry based methods: these methods are based on some geometric measure in the feature space.

A similar idea based on the K-centroids of the input data was used in <cit.>. * Uncertainty based methods: the aim of such methods is to find the most “difficult" examples, defined as the ones for which the model is the least confident.

Different uncertainty measures can be used for this purpose, see <cit.> for more details. * Error based methods: the goal is to find the most significant examples defined as the ones that contribute the most to the loss.

records.title: Repeated Random Sampling for Minimizing the Time-to-Accuracy of Learning

problem.text: Existing data pruning and distillation strategies come with high computational costs and often under-perform random sampling in high data compression regimes.

evidence.quote: Methods for carefully selecting or generating a small set of training data to learn from, i.e., data pruning, coreset selection, and data distillation, have been shown to be effective in reducing the ever-increasing cost of training neural networks.

However, these strategies come with additional computational costs associated with subset selection or data distillation before training begins, and furthermore, many are shown to even under-perform random sampling in high data compression regimes.

method.text: The authors introduce Repeated Sampling of Random Subsets (RS2), which samples a subset uniformly at random for each training epoch.

evidence.quote: In this work, we revisit a powerful yet overlooked random sampling strategy to address these challenges and introduce an approach called Repeated Sampling of Random Subsets (RSRS or RS2), where we randomly sample the subset of training data for each epoch of model training.
Motivated by this gap, we introduce Repeated Sampling of Random Subsets (RSRS = RS2), where we sample a subset uniformly at random for each training epoch.

results.text: RS2 reaches higher accuracy than existing methods across a wide range of pruning ratios, trains the fastest, and is robust to noisy labels.

evidence.quote: We show that: * Across a wide range of pruning ratios, RS2 reaches higher accuracy than all existing methods. * For a given pruning ratio, RS2 also trains the fastest, and thus has the fastest time-to-accuracy. * In the presence of noisy labels, RS2 is the most robust data pruning method; It achieves the highest end-model accuracy and lowest relative drop in performance vs. training on the clean dataset.

limitations.text: The authors identify a gap between RS2 and training on the full dataset and seek to overcome limitations of data pruning when training with SGD.

evidence.quote: Specifically, we are excited for future work focused on the following question: How can we further close the gap between RS2 and training on the full dataset?
Can we overcome this limitation of data pruning when training with SGD without eliminating the runtime benefits?

contributions.text: The authors introduce RS2, test it against state-of-the-art methods, and provide a convergence analysis.
